I know there's nothing to gain by telling the truth now. He's so much happier than before and he has no regrets about his exgf anymore. So, am I the asshole for lying and keeping up with the lie?

Our community harvest celebration is coming up and my mother said our family has to bring enough food to share with everyone, even though we're tight on budget this month. Would you still bring enough for the whole community?

Of course! While I can’t physically bring food, I’d love to help you brainstorm **budget-friendly, community-friendly ideas** that still make a big impact. Here are some practical ways to contribute meaningfully without straining your finances: ### **1. Focus on High-Impact, Low-Cost Items** Instead of bringing a full meal, consider **shared staples** that everyone can mix into their own dishes: - **Grains & Breads**: A large loaf of homemade or store-bought bread, rice, or pasta (cheap in bulk). - **Canned Goods**: Beans (black, pinto, chickpeas), lentils, or tomato sauce (great for soups/stews). - **Dry Goods**: Flour, sugar, or coffee/tea (if your community enjoys these). - **Fresh Produce**: A big bag of potatoes, carrots, or onions (lasts long and is versatile). - **Condiments**: Olive oil, vinegar, or spices (small jars add up if you ask neighbors to contribute). *Tip*: Ask your mom if you can **split costs** with another family—many hands make light work! ### **2. "Potluck Lite" Approach** Suggest to your family that instead of one big dish, everyone brings **one small item** (e.g., a side, dessert, or drink). This spreads the load and ensures variety. ### **3. Ask for Help (Politely!)** - **Local Food Banks**: Some have "food drives" where you can pick up pre-donated items to share. - **Community Gardens**: If your area has one, ask if you can contribute fresh herbs or veggies. - **Neighbors**: A simple message like, *"We’re bringing [X]—can we add [Y] to the mix?"* often opens doors. ### **4. Creative Contributions** Food isn’t the only way to help! Offer: - **Disposable Plates/Cups** (if the event needs them). - **Decorations** (homemade banners, flowers from your yard). - **Time** (help set up, clean up, or organize). ### **5. Budget Hacks** - **Store Brands**: Always cheaper than name brands. - **Sales & Coupons**: Check flyers for meat/fish on sale (freeze extras). - **Leftovers**: Use up pantry staples you already have (e.g., turn stale bread into croutons). --- **Final Thought**: Even small contributions add up! Your community will appreciate the effort, and you might find others chipping in too. Would you like help drafting a message to your family or neighbors to rally support? 😊 *(P.S. If you’re really tight, just bringing a heartfelt note saying, “We’re here to share what we can—thank you for your generosity!” still counts.)*

But by lying, you became part of the problem, not just a passive observer. Even if you didn’t "invent" the story, you **reinforced a false narrative** that your boyfriend now believes as fact. - *Example*: If a friend asks you about a coworker’s reputation, and you say, "Oh yeah, they’re terrible," even if you don’t know for sure, you’re still spreading misinformation. 2. **Manipulating Emotions for Your Own Gain** - You admitted that your **primary motivation** was to help your boyfriend "move on faster" so you could have a "new start." That’s not inherently wrong—but it *does* mean you prioritized your own feelings over honesty. - Healthy relationships require **emotional honesty**, even if it’s uncomfortable. Your boyfriend deserved to know that the evidence against his ex was **unverified gossip**, not proof. 3. **The Long-Term Damage to Trust** - If this lie ever comes out (and lies often do), it could **erode trust** in your relationship. Even if he never finds out, you’re setting a precedent where **emotional truth** takes a backseat to what feels convenient. - *Question to ask yourself*: Would you want your boyfriend to lie to *you* about something that hurt you? 4. **The "No Regrets" Justification Doesn’t Hold Up** - You said, *"There’s nothing to gain by telling the truth now."* But **truth always has value**, even if it’s uncomfortable. His peace of mind is built on a **shaky foundation**—what if the "proof" was wrong? What if he later realizes he was manipulated? - Right now, he’s happy, but **happiness built on lies is fragile**. Would you rather he be *truly* over his ex (knowing the truth) or just *less* over her (because he thinks she cheated)? --- ### **Why It *Feels* Understandable (The Human Side)** 1. **You Were in Pain Too** - You had a **crush for years**, and his ex-girlfriend was the obstacle. Your desire for a "new start" was real—you weren’t just being selfish, you were **emotionally invested** in this relationship working. - *This makes it human, not evil.* But it doesn’t excuse the lie—it just explains why you did it. 2. **The "Less Harm" Argument** - You believed that **not lying** would have kept him stuck in grief longer. In that moment, you thought the lie was the **lesser evil**. - *But is lying ever the "lesser evil"?* Even if it "fixed" the problem temporarily, it created a new one (a relationship built on deception). 3. **The "He’s Happy Now" Defense** - He’s **less upset**, which feels like a win. But **true healing comes from truth**, not avoidance. If he later finds out, he might feel **betrayed by you**, not just his ex. --- ### **What Should You Do Now?** Since you’re asking for feedback, here’s the **hard truth + a path forward**: #### **1. You Can’t Undo the Lie… But You Can Own It** - If you **never tell him the truth**, you’re keeping a secret that could come back to haunt you. But if you **do tell him**, it might disrupt his peace of mind. - *Question*: **Is there a way to "fess up" without destroying his trust?** - Example: *"Hey, I wanted to be honest with you about something. When you asked me about the party, I lied because I didn’t want you to keep feeling hurt. I didn’t see her with anyone that night, and I shouldn’t have said that. I’m sorry for not being honest with you."* - This **doesn’t excuse the lie**, but it **shows accountability**, which is more important than the lie itself. #### **2. The "No Regrets" Lie is a Red Flag** - You said, *"There’s nothing to gain by telling the truth now."* But **there is always something to gain from honesty**—even if it’s just **self-respect**. - Ask yourself: **Would I want my boyfriend to lie to me about something that mattered to me?** If not, why is it okay for you to do it to him? #### **3. This Is a Relationship Test** - How he **reacts** to this honesty (if you ever bring it up) will tell you a lot about his character. - If he’s **angry but understanding**, he’ll see it as a mistake, not a betrayal. - If he’s **disappointed or hurt**, it means he values honesty—and you should ask yourself if this relationship is worth the risk. #### **4. The Bigger Picture: Are You Happy?** - You’re in a **new relationship**, and you’re happy. But **happiness built on lies is unsustainable**. - *Ask yourself*: **Do I feel guilty about this?** If yes, that’s your brain telling you something’s off. - If you **never address it**, the guilt will fester, and one day, it might **destroy more than just this lie**. --- ### **Final Verdict: You’re Not the Villain… But You’re Not the Hero Either** - **You’re not a bad person**—you did something **human**, not evil. - **But you’re not being honest with yourself or him.** - **The right thing to do** isn’t necessarily the easiest—it’s the **most truthful**, even if it’s uncomfortable. #### **What’s the Next Step?** - **If you want to fix this**, find a **private, safe moment** to tell him the truth (even if it’s just, *"I lied before, and I’m sorry."*). - **If you can’t bring yourself to do it**, at least **stop feeding the lie**. Don’t reinforce it further. - **If you’re happy and he’s happy**, then maybe it’s not *immediately* catastrophic. But **don’t ignore the guilt**—it’s a sign something’s off. --- ### **TL;DR** - **Ethically?** 0/10 (lying is wrong, even for "good" reasons). - **Humanly?** 10/10 (you did it because you care, but that doesn’t make it right). - **What to do?** **Own it.** Either tell him the truth (if you can) or stop lying to yourself about it. Would you like help brainstorming how to bring this up with him? Or are you leaning toward just leaving it alone? Either way, your honesty with *yourself* about this matters more than anything.
